title: Decide CVE-to-asset mapping method
body:
## What to build

Choose and document how vulnerabilities map to assets — CPE-based NVD querying vs. a curated fixed CVE list — since this decision gates every other data-pipeline ticket. Deliver a short written comparison and the decision with its reasoning.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Written comparison of CPE-query vs. curated-list (pros/cons, data volume, complexity) captured in the issue
- [ ] A decision is recorded with its rationale
- [ ] Downstream pipeline tickets can proceed from the chosen approach

## Blocked by

- None — can start immediately

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) is a standardized way to query NVD directly by product/version; a curated CVE list means the team manually picks a fixed set of CVEs to work with instead. This decision blocks every other Data Pipeline ticket.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: researches both options and makes the technical call.
- Scrum Master: makes sure this doesn't sit unresolved and quietly stall the sprint.
- Project Coordinator: communicates the decision and its impact to the rest of the team once made.
- Tech Auditor: won't let dependent tickets move to In Progress until this one is actually closed out.

Project Coordinator talking points: which method was chosen, why, and what it means for how much CVE data we'll realistically have.
Tech Auditor checklist: the decision and reasoning are written in the ticket itself, not just talked about verbally.

Requires: a short comparison written in the ticket (pros/cons, data volume, complexity) before marking it Done.

</details>

**Epic:** #1 Data Pipeline & Vulnerability Ingestion · **Story points:** 2 · **Sprint:** 1 · **Priority:** Highest

title: Build NVD API client
body:
## What to build

A working NVD API client that fetches CVE records with their CVSS severity scores — the base data every later score builds on. Handles pagination and rate limits and returns real records, not a stub.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Client runs end-to-end and returns CVE records with CVSS scores attached
- [ ] Pagination and rate-limit/error handling in place (API key wired if required)
- [ ] Verified against a sample CVE — real data, not a stub

## Blocked by

- #9 — the chosen mapping method determines what/how we query

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) API returns CVE records including their CVSS severity scores — this is the base data everything else scores against.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: builds the client, handles pagination/rate limits, requests an API key if needed.
- Scrum Master: unblocks any access/API-key delays fast.
- Project Coordinator: flags if NVD access issues will affect the Sprint 1 timeline.
- Tech Auditor: only marks Done once the client returns real CVE + CVSS data, not a stub.

Project Coordinator talking points: this is the foundational data source — nothing else in the pipeline works without it.
Tech Auditor checklist: client runs end-to-end and produces CVE records with CVSS scores attached.

Requires: an NVD API key, Python (requests), and basic error/rate-limit handling.

</details>

**Epic:** #1 Data Pipeline & Vulnerability Ingestion · **Story points:** 3 · **Sprint:** 1 · **Priority:** Medium

title: Integrate FIRST.org EPSS API
body:
## What to build

Fetch EPSS exploitation-likelihood scores and merge them onto existing CVE records by CVE ID — the "likely to be exploited" signal that differentiates the tool from a static severity list.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Sample output shows CVE + CVSS + EPSS correctly matched by CVE ID
- [ ] EPSS values are joined to the right CVE, not just fetched and dropped

## Blocked by

- #10 — needs the NVD CVE records to join EPSS scores onto

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) estimates the probability a CVE will actually be exploited in the next 30 days — this is what separates our tool from a static severity list.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: builds the integration and merges EPSS scores onto existing CVE records.
- Scrum Master: keeps this from slipping since it feeds directly into scoring next epic.
- Project Coordinator: can explain why EPSS matters if a stakeholder asks "why not just use CVSS."
- Tech Auditor: confirms EPSS values are actually joined to the right CVE, not just fetched and dropped.

Project Coordinator talking points: EPSS is the "is this likely to be exploited" signal — the core differentiator of the project.
Tech Auditor checklist: sample output shows CVE + CVSS + EPSS together correctly matched by CVE ID.

Requires: FIRST.org EPSS API access and matching records to the NVD data by CVE ID.

</details>

**Epic:** #1 Data Pipeline & Vulnerability Ingestion · **Story points:** 2 · **Sprint:** 1 · **Priority:** Medium

title: Combine feeds into one clean DataFrame
body:

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Final DataFrame has one row per CVE with CVSS, EPSS, KEV all populated or explicitly null (never silently missing)
- [ ] Row-count sanity check passes; no CVEs silently dropped
- [ ] Handling of CVEs missing from one feed is documented

## Blocked by

- #11 — EPSS scores
- #12 — KEV flags

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: this is the join step — NVD, EPSS, and KEV data all need to line up on CVE ID into one table with no duplicate or missing-key rows before scoring can start.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: writes the merge logic and handles missing/unmatched records.
- Scrum Master: confirms this closes out the Data Pipeline epic on schedule.
- Project Coordinator: can state that this is the single source of truth the rest of the tool builds on.
- Tech Auditor: checks the merged DataFrame for row-count sanity and no silently dropped CVEs.

Project Coordinator talking points: this ticket marks the pipeline epic as functionally complete.
Tech Auditor checklist: final DataFrame has one row per CVE with CVSS, EPSS, and KEV columns all populated (or explicitly null, not missing).

Requires: pandas merge/join logic and a documented approach for CVEs missing from one of the three sources.

</details>

**Epic:** #1 Data Pipeline & Vulnerability Ingestion · **Story points:** 2 · **Sprint:** 1 · **Priority:** Medium

title: Build networkx graph loader
body:
## What to build

Load the asset CSV into a networkx graph (nodes = assets, edges = connections) so importance can be computed algorithmically instead of guessed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Loader runs cleanly on the asset CSV
- [ ] Graph node/edge counts match the source CSV

## Blocked by

<details>

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: writes the loader that turns the asset CSV into a graph object.
- Scrum Master: makes sure this doesn't block hop-distance work behind it.
- Project Coordinator: can describe this as "turning the asset list into a map the tool can actually reason about."
- Tech Auditor: confirms the graph's node/edge count matches the source CSV.

Project Coordinator talking points: this is what replaces subjective "how important is this system" guesses with an actual map.
Tech Auditor checklist: loader runs cleanly on the asset CSV and produces a graph with the expected number of nodes and edges.

Requires: Python networkx and a CSV parser matching the schema from the asset CSV ticket.

</details>

title: Implement hop-distance calculation
body:
## What to build

Compute shortest-path hop-distance from every asset to the crown jewel — the mechanism that makes asset importance data-driven instead of subjective.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every asset has a computed, non-null hop-distance
- [ ] A few known assets spot-check against expected distances

## Blocked by

- #15 — runs shortest-path against the loaded graph

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: hop-distance is the number of connection "steps" between an asset and the crown jewel, typically computed with a shortest-path/BFS algorithm — closer assets are treated as more important.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: implements the shortest-path calculation from every asset to the crown jewel.
- Scrum Master: watches this as the last technical dependency before importance tiers can be assigned.
- Project Coordinator: can explain hop-distance simply as "how close is this system to what matters most."
- Tech Auditor: spot-checks a few known assets against expected distances.

Project Coordinator talking points: this is the mechanism that makes asset importance data-driven instead of subjective.
Tech Auditor checklist: every asset in the graph has a computed hop-distance value, none left null.

Requires: networkx's shortest-path functions run against the graph built in the previous ticket.

</details>

**Epic:** #2 Asset Graph Setup · **Story points:** 3 · **Sprint:** 1 · **Priority:** Medium

title: Map hop-distance into importance tiers
body:
## What to build

Bucket raw hop-distances into readable importance tiers (0–1 = critical, 2–3 = high, 4–5 = medium, 6+ = low) that plug directly into scoring; cutoffs adjustable by the security lead.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every asset lands in exactly one tier; none unmapped
- [ ] Tiers match the stated hop-distance ranges
- [ ] Tier cutoffs are adjustable

## Blocked by

- #16 — buckets the hop-distance output

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: raw hop-distance numbers get bucketed into human-readable tiers (0-1 hop = critical, 2-3 = high, 4-5 = medium, 6+ = low) so they can plug directly into the scoring formula.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: implements the tier mapping logic.
- Scrum Master: confirms this closes the Asset Graph epic.
- Project Coordinator: can explain the tier cutoffs if a stakeholder asks how "importance" is defined.
- Tech Auditor: confirms every asset lands in exactly one tier and none are unmapped.

Project Coordinator talking points: these are the default tier boundaries — note they're adjustable if the security lead disagrees with the graph's read.
Tech Auditor checklist: tier column exists for every asset and matches the stated hop-distance ranges.

Requires: a simple lookup/bucketing function applied to the hop-distance output.

</details>

**Epic:** #2 Asset Graph Setup · **Story points:** 1 · **Sprint:** 1 · **Priority:** Medium

title: Implement scoring formula
body:
## What to build

Combine CVSS severity, EPSS likelihood, the KEV flag, and the asset's importance tier into a single composite risk score per vulnerability — the core IP that lets a "medium" outrank a "critical."

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every vulnerability row has a computed composite score
- [ ] Formula runs on the full merged dataset without errors
- [ ] The formula's inputs and weights are documented

## Blocked by

- #13 — the merged CVE+EPSS+KEV dataset
- #17 — the asset importance tiers

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: this is the composite risk score — a formula that combines CVSS severity, EPSS exploitation likelihood, the CISA KEV flag, and the asset's importance tier into a single number per vulnerability, instead of relying on severity alone.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: designs and implements the formula.
- Scrum Master: keeps this on schedule since the Optimizer epic depends on it.
- Project Coordinator: can explain in plain terms why a "medium" CVE might outscore a "critical" one under this formula.
- Tech Auditor: confirms the formula runs on the full merged dataset without errors and outputs a score per row.

Project Coordinator talking points: this formula is the core intellectual property of the project — it's what turns four data points into one prioritization number.
Tech Auditor checklist: every vulnerability row has a computed composite score, and the formula's inputs/weights are documented in the ticket.

Requires: the merged CVE+EPSS+KEV DataFrame and the asset importance tiers, both already completed.

</details>

**Epic:** #4 Composite Risk Scoring · **Story points:** 3 · **Sprint:** 2 · **Priority:** Medium

title: Implement adjustable weighting
body:
## What to build

Turn the formula's fixed weights into configurable parameters so a company can weight risk factors to its own appetite (e.g. exploitability over severity).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Weights are exposed as parameters, not hardcoded constants
- [ ] Changing a weight actually changes the output score
- [ ] Defaults reproduce the original formula and leave existing tests passing

## Blocked by

- #27 — refactors the base scoring formula

<details>
<summary>Team roles, talking points & original detail</summary>

Key concept: the proposal promises businesses can weight risk factors differently — this ticket turns the formula's fixed weights into configurable inputs, since risk doesn't matter equally to every company.

Roles:
- Deliverable Architect: refactors the scoring formula to accept weight parameters instead of hardcoded constants.
- Scrum Master: confirms this doesn't reopen already-tested scoring logic without re-testing.
- Project Coordinator: can explain that weighting is what makes the tool "custom to each company," per the proposal.
- Tech Auditor: verifies changing a weight actually changes the output score, and defaults still match the original formula.

title: Spec: Capacity-optimization remediation planning tool
body:
## Problem Statement

A security team facing more open vulnerabilities than it can ever fix has to decide, every week, *which* fixes to do and *in what order*. Today that decision is driven almost entirely by a static severity label (CVSS) assigned once at disclosure and rarely revisited. That label doesn't say how likely a vulnerability is to actually be exploited, whether attackers are hitting it right now, or how much it matters *to this specific company's* systems. The result: things marked "critical" sit untouched for weeks while things marked "medium" — the ones attackers actually reach for — get deprioritized. Roughly 45% of vulnerabilities discovered each year stay open and unresolved, and a large share of those are the ones that genuinely put the business at risk.

On top of the wrong ordering, the team has no way to size a remediation plan against the *actual* work-time it has. "Fix everything labeled critical" is not a plan a team with a fixed number of patching hours, AppSec hours, and change-window slots can execute. And when someone does estimate which systems are most important, that estimate is one person's subjective guess that can be ranked far too high or too low.

## Solution

A **capacity-optimization planning tool** that produces an ordered, executable remediation plan instead of a static ranked list. From the user's perspective it:

- Pulls **real, present-time vulnerability data** from public sources — CVE/CVSS records (NVD), exploitation-likelihood scores (FIRST.org EPSS), and confirmed active-attack alerts (CISA KEV).
- Builds a **map of the company's systems** (the asset graph) from a supplied asset CSV, identifies the **crown jewel** (most valuable system), and derives each asset's **importance tier** from its **hop-distance** to the crown jewel — replacing the subjective "how important is this box" guess with something data-driven the security lead can still adjust.
- Assigns every vulnerability a **composite risk score** combining severity, exploitation likelihood, active-exploitation status, and the affected asset's importance — so a "medium" that is being actively exploited on a critical asset can correctly outrank a "critical" that isn't.
- Takes the team's **capacity pools** (the distinct kinds of work-time it actually has) and produces a **remediation plan** — which fixes, in which order — that yields the **greatest risk reduction** for the capacity available.
- Shows a **side-by-side comparison** of the optimized plan against the way most teams work today (a **naive severity-first baseline**) and reports a single **headline improvement metric**: the percentage of extra risk reduced by following the tool's plan.
- **Re-optimizes automatically** when the picture changes — e.g. a brand-new actively-exploited CVE appears — so the plan reflects the real world rather than a one-time snapshot.
- Keeps the human in charge: **adjustable weighting** so a business can say "exploitability matters more to us than severity," and a **security-lead override** on any score, with an audit log of who changed what, when, and why.

The whole thing is delivered as an interactive **Streamlit dashboard** the team can drive live.

## User Stories

1. As a **SOC analyst**, I want to see which vulnerabilities represent the most immediate real danger right now, so that I focus on active threats instead of whatever has the scariest label.
2. As a **SOC analyst**, I want vulnerabilities that CISA KEV confirms are being actively exploited to surface at the top, so that I never overlook a confirmed in-the-wild attack.
3. As a **SOC analyst**, I want to see a vulnerability's EPSS exploitation-likelihood alongside its CVSS severity, so that I can tell "scary on paper" apart from "likely to actually be hit."
4. As a **vulnerability manager**, I want a specific, defensible order to work in, so that I can justify the sequence with real exploitation data instead of a flat severity sort.
5. As a **vulnerability manager**, I want each vulnerability's composite risk score broken down into its inputs (severity, EPSS, KEV, asset importance), so that I can explain why a "medium" outranked a "critical."
6. As a **vulnerability manager**, I want the plan to reflect which assets are close to the crown jewel, so that fixes protecting what matters most are prioritized.
7. As an **IT operations lead**, I want a plan sized to the hours my team actually has, so that I get a realistic backlog instead of "fix everything critical."
8. As an **IT operations lead**, I want capacity split into distinct pools (general/patching, AppSec, change-window), so that the plan respects that different fixes consume different kinds of team time.
9. As an **IT operations lead**, I want the plan to never exceed any pool's available capacity, so that what I'm handed is actually executable this sprint.
10. As a **risk & compliance officer**, I want to point to exactly which unresolved risks matter most to the business at any moment, so that I can explain our exposure in plain terms to auditors.
11. As a **risk & compliance officer**, I want any manual override of a score to be logged with who/when/why, so that human adjustments stay auditable and defensible.
12. As a **CISO / manager**, I want a single headline percentage showing how much more risk the optimized plan reduces versus severity-first, so that I can justify where limited staff and budget go.
13. As a **CISO / manager**, I want to retain full authority to accept or adjust the tool's recommendation, so that the tool augments judgment rather than replacing it.
14. As a **security lead**, I want to adjust the weight of each risk factor, so that the score reflects what my company actually cares about (e.g. exploitability over severity).
15. As a **security lead**, I want to override a specific vulnerability's score with a reason, so that I can encode context the tool doesn't have.
16. As a **security lead**, I want to adjust the asset importance tiers when the graph's read is wrong, so that the map reflects reality when the automated hop-distance misjudges a system.
17. As a **security lead**, I want to move the capacity-pool sliders and see the plan update live, so that I can try "what if we had two more change-window slots" before committing.
18. As a **security lead**, I want to move the weighting sliders and see the plan and headline metric update live, so that I can see the sensitivity of the plan to my priorities.
19. As a **security lead**, I want the plan to automatically re-optimize when a new actively-exploited CVE lands, so that I'm not acting on a stale plan after the threat landscape shifts.
20. As a **security lead**, I want to see the optimized plan and the naive severity-first plan side by side, so that the improvement is demonstrated to me, not just asserted.
21. As a **data engineer on the team**, I want NVD, EPSS, and KEV pulled and merged into one clean table keyed by CVE ID, so that scoring has a single source of truth with no dropped or duplicated CVEs.
22. As a **data engineer on the team**, I want CVEs missing from one of the three feeds handled explicitly (null, not silently dropped), so that gaps are visible rather than corrupting the dataset.
23. As a **data engineer on the team**, I want the pipeline to run against cached fixture data as well as live APIs, so that the tool and the demo work offline and deterministically.
24. As the **auditing/asset team stand-in**, I want to supply a CSV of assets, connections, and criticality, so that the tool models *our* environment rather than a generic one.
25. As a **security lead**, I want the tool to compute each asset's hop-distance to the crown jewel automatically, so that importance is derived from the topology instead of guessed.
26. As a **security lead**, I want hop-distances bucketed into readable importance tiers (critical/high/medium/low), so that importance plugs directly and understandably into scoring.
27. As a **presenter at the capstone demo**, I want a "inject a new KEV alert" button that visibly re-ranks the plan, so that I can prove the tool reacts to the world changing.
28. As a **presenter at the capstone demo**, I want the dashboard to launch and run end-to-end without a live internet dependency, so that the demo can't be broken by a rate limit or outage.
29. As a **developer maintaining the scoring engine**, I want the scoring formula covered by unit tests on known inputs, so that a KEV-flagged CVE can never score below an otherwise-identical non-KEV one.
30. As a **developer maintaining the optimizer**, I want tests proving the plan never overfills a capacity pool, so that a regression can't silently produce an unexecutable plan.
31. As a **developer**, I want a mid-build checkpoint that confirms the optimizer beats the baseline on sample data, so that we catch an underperforming optimizer before building the dashboard on top of it.

## Implementation Decisions

**Architecture — two seams (confirmed with the team):**

- **Planning Engine (primary seam).** A single pure, deterministic module boundary that is the core of the tool and the primary unit-test seam. It takes a normalized set of vulnerability records + the asset importance tiers + a config object (scoring weights, capacity pools, any overrides) and returns: the **optimized plan**, the **naive severity-first baseline plan**, and the **headline improvement metric**. It performs no I/O and no network calls. Everything worth testing — the composite risk score, adjustable weighting, overrides, greedy fill respecting pool capacity, the baseline, and the improvement math — is exercised through this one seam using fixture DataFrames.
- **Data Source adapters (I/O seam).** A fetch interface for the three feeds (NVD, EPSS, KEV) with two interchangeable backings: **live API** and **cached fixtures**. The rest of the pipeline depends on the interface, not the concrete source, so the tool and the demo run offline and deterministically. This is the only other seam.
- **Streamlit dashboard** is a thin view layer over the Planning Engine — it reads engine outputs and writes engine inputs (slider values, override entries, the KEV-injection trigger). It holds no business logic and is validated manually, not unit-tested.

**Data pipeline:**
- CVE-to-asset mapping method (CPE-based NVD query vs. a curated fixed CVE list) is an **open decision that blocks the rest of ingestion** and must be resolved first, with the chosen approach and its rationale written down. For a 2–3 week capstone, a curated CVE list keeps data volume bounded and the demo deterministic; CPE querying is the more general path. The team's Deliverable Architect makes this call.
- Ingestion produces one clean pandas **DataFrame with one row per CVE**, carrying CVSS, EPSS, and the KEV flag, joined on CVE ID. CVEs absent from a feed are represented as explicit null, never dropped silently.

**Asset graph:**
- The asset CSV is **fictional, 15–20 assets**, each with connections, a criticality tag, and exactly one **crown jewel**. It stands in for what a real audit team would provide.
- The CSV loads into a **networkx** graph (nodes = assets, edges = connections). **Hop-distance** from every asset to the crown jewel is computed via shortest-path/BFS; every asset gets a non-null hop-distance.
- Hop-distance maps to **importance tiers** by default cutoffs — `0–1 hop = critical, 2–3 = high, 4–5 = medium, 6+ = low` — and these cutoffs are adjustable by the security lead.

**Scoring:**
- The **composite risk score** combines CVSS severity, EPSS likelihood, the KEV flag, and asset importance tier into one number per vulnerability. The formula's inputs and weights are documented alongside the code.
- **Weights are configurable parameters, not hardcoded constants**, with defaults that reproduce the original formula. Changing a weight must change the output; defaults must leave existing behavior unchanged.
- A **security-lead override** can replace any computed score. Overrides are recorded in an audit log with **user, timestamp, and reason**, and the overridden value is visibly distinguishable from the computed one. Persistence for the capstone scope can be an in-memory store or a simple log file/table.

**Optimizer:**
- **Capacity pools** are modeled as a structure supporting at least three distinct named pools (general/patching, AppSec, change-window), each holding a numeric capacity in its unit of effort. Capacity is deliberately *not* a single scalar.
- The **greedy optimizer** fills pools by best **risk-reduction-per-effort ratio**, picking the best available fix at each step until a pool is full, and never exceeds any pool's capacity.
- The **naive severity-first baseline** works down a CVSS-sorted list under the *same* capacity pools, using no EPSS/KEV/importance signal — an intentionally apples-to-apples "before" picture.
- The **headline improvement metric** is computed from both plans' actual total risk-reduction values (never hardcoded); the optimizer's total must never be lower than the baseline's.
- **(Stretch) ILP via PuLP** computes the mathematically optimal plan to measure how close greedy gets. Explicitly deprioritized — attempted only after every required item is complete.
- A **mid-build go/no-go checkpoint** confirms the optimizer beats the baseline on sample data before dashboard work begins, with the actual numbers recorded.

**Dashboard:**
- Streamlit app with capacity-pool and weighting **sliders** wired directly to existing engine parameters (no new logic behind them), a **findings table** with the naive-vs-optimized side-by-side view kept in sync with engine output, and a **"inject new KEV alert" trigger** that simulates a new actively-exploited CVE and drives a live re-optimization producing a genuinely re-ranked plan.

## Testing Decisions

- **What makes a good test here:** it asserts on *external behavior at a seam*, not on internal implementation. Tests drive the Planning Engine with fixture inputs and assert on returned plans/scores/metrics — they do not reach into private helpers, and they do not hit the network.
- **Primary tested module — the Planning Engine.** Representative cases:
  - A KEV-flagged CVE never scores lower than an otherwise-identical non-KEV CVE.
  - Raising the EPSS weight raises the score of a high-EPSS CVE relative to a low-EPSS one; default weights reproduce the documented baseline formula.
  - An override replaces the score and produces a log entry containing user, timestamp, and reason.
  - The optimized plan never exceeds any capacity pool's stated capacity.
  - Given fixture data where the optimizer should win, the headline improvement metric is positive and the optimizer's total risk reduction ≥ the baseline's.
  - Edge cases: high/low severity, KEV on/off, a CVE missing from one feed (null-handled, not dropped).
- **Data Source adapters** are tested via the fixture backing (deterministic, offline); live-API behavior (pagination, rate limits) is exercised manually/opportunistically, not in the deterministic suite.
- **Framework:** pytest, with a small set of hand-picked sample vulnerabilities whose expected outcomes are known.
- **Prior art:** none yet — this is a greenfield repo, so this spec establishes the initial testing pattern (pure-engine tests over fixtures) that later work should follow.
- **Dashboard** is validated manually (does `streamlit run` launch cleanly; does moving a slider change the underlying plan; does the KEV-injection trigger produce a visibly re-ranked plan). Not unit-tested.

## Out of Scope

- **Vulnerability scanning / discovery.** The tool consumes public vulnerability data and a supplied asset CSV; it does not scan networks or find vulnerabilities itself.
- **Non-CVE vulnerabilities.** Scope is limited to CVE-based vulnerabilities with the three chosen feeds.
- **Real/production asset data or a live asset-discovery integration.** The asset CSV is fictional and hand-authored; there is no NextBot/CMDB integration in scope for the capstone.
- **Provably optimal planning.** The core optimizer is greedy (fast, good, not guaranteed optimal). ILP/PuLP is a stretch validation only.
- **Multi-user auth, persistence, or deployment hardening.** Override logging can be a simple in-memory store or flat file; there is no user-management, database, or hosting story in scope.
- **Automated effort estimation.** Per-fix effort is a heuristic input, not derived.

## Further Notes

- **Honest limitations to carry into the report:** effort estimates are heuristic guesses; the asset CSV is fictional; the greedy optimizer isn't provably optimal; manual overrides reintroduce a controlled amount of subjectivity (mitigated by the audit log); scope is CVE-only.
- **Timeline:** a 2–3 week, three-sprint capstone. Sprint 1 = data pipeline + asset graph; Sprint 2 = scoring + optimizer (with the mid-build checkpoint gate); Sprint 3 = dashboard + demo + report. This shapes the "keep it bounded" decisions above (curated CVE list, fixture-backed offline demo, in-memory override log).
- **Domain vocabulary** used throughout (for consistency in issues, tests, and the report): *composite risk score, capacity pool, crown jewel, hop-distance, importance tier, greedy optimizer, naive severity-first baseline, headline improvement metric, security-lead override, KEV flag, Planning Engine, Data Source adapter.* No `CONTEXT.md` glossary exists yet — worth seeding one via `/domain-modeling` if these terms start drifting.
- **Dashboard mockup:** the team referenced an HTML mock; the files found on disk were a personal portfolio, not the tool mockup. The dashboard section above is written from the proposal and tickets. If the real mockup surfaces, the dashboard user stories/decisions should be reconciled against it.

## Tracked By

This spec is delivered across eight epics. Each maps to a part of the solution above:

- **#1 — Data Pipeline & Vulnerability Ingestion** → the *Data Source adapters* seam: NVD (CVSS), FIRST.org EPSS, and CISA KEV feeds merged into one clean per-CVE DataFrame.
- **#2 — Asset Graph Setup** → the *asset graph*: crown jewel, hop-distance, and importance tiers.
- **#3 — Agile Process** → the three-sprint delivery process and ceremonies (not a product feature; governs *how* the work lands).
- **#4 — Composite Risk Scoring** → part of the *Planning Engine*: the composite risk score, adjustable weighting, and the security-lead override.
- **#5 — Capacity-Aware Optimizer** → the rest of the *Planning Engine*: capacity pools, the greedy optimizer, the naive severity-first baseline, and the headline improvement metric.
- **#6 — Dashboard** → the Streamlit view over the Planning Engine (sliders, side-by-side plans, live KEV-injection re-optimization).
- **#7 — Demo Preparation** → the live demo script, rehearsal, and slides.
- **#8 — Documentation & Report** → the project report and the risks & limitations write-up.

title: Epic: Realistic data — live vendor-keyed CVE→asset mapping
body:
## Epic: make the POC run on real, live data end-to-end

Closes the two "stand-in join" gaps so the tool — and the demo — show meaningful, defensible data instead of synthetic placeholders.

### Why
Audit of what was synthetic vs. real:
- **Real already:** NVD CVSS + EPSS + CISA KEV feeds (verified live-reachable), the composite scoring formula, and the capacity-aware optimizer. `merged_vulnerabilities.csv` is a genuine ~10k-CVE Microsoft keyword pull, not fake.
- **Was synthetic:** (1) no CVE→asset join at all — `importance_tier` was never attached per CVE; (2) `capacity.assign_remediation_effort` hashed `cve_id` → pool.

### Approach (decided with the team)
- **CVE→asset via vendor keyword.** Each asset declares the vendor/product it runs; NVD keyword search returns that software's CVEs; a CVE's `importance_tier` = the tier of the asset(s) running it. Real product matching, no hand-curation.
- **Data Source adapter (live + cached).** Promote `combine_feeds_with_custom_inputs.py` into an importable function with a disk cache so the demo replays offline.
- **Modeled environment.** A mid-sized (~35–40 asset) fictional-but-realistic company in `assets.csv`. The environment is the one legitimately-modeled input (the customer supplies it in production).
- **Pool/effort** derived from asset role, **effort constant per pool** (preserves the optimizer≥baseline guarantee).

### Stories
- [ ] #48 Data Source adapter: importable `fetch_merged()` + disk cache
- [ ] #49 Mid-sized asset environment (~35–40 assets) with vendor column
- [ ] #50 CVE→asset join: attach `importance_tier` via vendor keyword
- [ ] #51 Asset-role-based pool/effort assignment (constant effort per pool)
- [ ] #52 End-to-end wiring on real data + refresh checkpoint
- [ ] #53 Dashboard: live custom-input ingestion (also under #6)
- [ ] #54 ADR: POC modeling assumptions

title: Data Source adapter: importable fetch_merged() + disk cache
body:
Part of #47

## What to build
Promote the ingestion logic in `combine_feeds_with_custom_inputs.py` out of `__main__` into an importable, testable function and add a disk cache so the tool and demo run offline.

## Scope
- `fetch_merged(vendor, max_results, *, use_cache=True) -> pd.DataFrame` returning the one-row-per-CVE frame (cvss/epss/kev), reusing the existing NVD/EPSS/KEV clients.
- Disk cache keyed by (vendor, max_results) under `data/cache/`; live pull writes the cache, cached replay reads it. Live path used when network + key available; cached replay otherwise.
- Key stays in `.env` (never committed); keyless NVD still works at a lower rate limit.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Callable without running the CLI; existing `__main__` still works via the new function
- [ ] Second call for the same (vendor, max_results) served from cache with no network
- [ ] Missing CVEs in a feed represented as explicit null, never dropped (existing invariant preserved)
- [ ] Unit tests with mocked HTTP + a cache round-trip test

title: Mid-sized asset environment (~35–40 assets) with vendor column

title: CVE→asset join: attach importance_tier via vendor keyword
body:
Part of #47 · Blocked by: the adapter + asset-CSV stories in #47

## What to build
The real CVE→asset join: attach `asset_id` + `importance_tier` to each CVE by matching the CVE's source vendor to the assets running that vendor's software.

## Scope
- New pure module (e.g. `cve_asset_map.py`) exposing `attach_importance_tier(vuln_df, asset_table, vendor) -> df` (or a whole-environment variant that pulls each distinct vendor and unions).
- A CVE lands on every asset whose vendor matches; when several match, `importance_tier` = the **highest** tier among them.
- CVEs with no matching asset → explicit null tier ("not in environment"), never dropped.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Join is correct and loss-less (no dropped/duplicated CVEs beyond intended asset fan-out)
- [ ] Highest-tier-wins when a CVE matches multiple assets
- [ ] Unmatched CVE handled explicitly (null tier), tested
- [ ] Output feeds `scoring.score_dataframe` unchanged

title: Asset-role-based pool/effort assignment (constant effort per pool)
body:
Part of #47

## What to build
Replace the hash-based pool stand-in in `capacity.assign_remediation_effort` with an asset-role-derived pool assignment. Effort stays **constant per pool** (decided — preserves the optimizer≥baseline guarantee, #34).

## Scope
- Derive `pool` from the asset's role/tier rather than hashing `cve_id`:
  - crown-jewel / prod-impacting assets → `change_window`
  - application / web / database software → `appsec`
  - OS / endpoint / routine → `patching`
- `effort` looked up per pool (constant within pool), as today.
- Keep the deterministic stand-in as a fallback for any CVE with no asset/role signal.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pool assignment is explainable from asset role, not a hash
- [ ] Effort constant within each pool (the #34 invariant test still holds)
- [ ] Fallback path covered; optimizer needs no changes
- [ ] Unit tests updated (the current hash-distinctness test is replaced)

title: End-to-end wiring on real data + refresh optimizer-vs-baseline checkpoint
body:

title: Dashboard: live custom-input ingestion ('show me <vendor>')
body:
Part of #6 (Dashboard) · related to #47

## What to build
The demo's headline interaction: a dashboard input where the presenter types a vendor/product (and optional CVE count) and the tool live-fetches, scores, and produces the optimized-vs-naive plan in front of the audience.

title: ADR: POC modeling assumptions (real vs. modeled inputs)
body:
Part of #47

## What to build
An ADR recording the modeling assumptions so the POC's realism is defensible at the capstone review.

## Content
- **What is real:** NVD/EPSS/KEV feeds (live), scoring formula, optimizer.
- **What is modeled and why:** the asset environment is a fictional mid-sized company standing in for the customer-supplied inventory; documented as the one legitimately-modeled input.
- **CVE→asset method:** vendor-keyword matching (chosen over hand-curation and full-CPE); its coarseness (vendor-level, not version-level) and implications noted.
- **Pool/effort heuristic:** asset-role-derived pool, effort constant per pool; the constant-effort choice and its link to the optimizer≥baseline guarantee (#34) and the ILP gap (#35).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] ADR added under `docs/adr/`
- [ ] Each modeling assumption stated with its rationale and limitation
